Interpret them as distinct SCOPe families inside one superfamily, not as one family. In SCOPe they sit in the all-alpha class (a), fold a.25 (ferritin-like, a four-helical bundle), superfamily a.25.1 (ferritin-like). Ferritins (including bacterioferritins and Dps-like relatives, a.25.1.1), ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins (the R2/class I RNR subunit family, with related di-iron oxygenase-like proteins) and manganese catalases (di-manganese T-catalases) are separate families. Superfamily placement means a common ancestor is inferred from structure plus a shared di-metal-binding site (the conserved Glu/Asp-x-x-His motifs on the helical bundle). The family split reflects lower sequence identity and functional divergence, so it is a remote-homology relationship. I am giving the family numbering from memory and can't check it against a specific SCOPe release (e.g., 2.08), so look up exact sccs and sunid values before citing them.

The chemistries differ. Ferritins are ferroxidase and iron-storage proteins: Fe(II) is oxidized by O2 or H2O2 at a dinuclear site, and the iron is mineralized in a 24-mer shell cavity. RNR R2 subunits use a di-iron site with O2 to make a tyrosyl radical (or a Mn/Fe cofactor in some subclasses) that starts radical chemistry in the R1 subunit. Manganese catalases use a di-Mn site to disproportionate H2O2 through Mn(II)2/Mn(III)2 cycling. This is functional divergence on a shared scaffold. The shared fold and metal-site architecture have been adapted to different substrates, redox states, oligomeric assemblies and partner proteins.

Limits on inference: SCOPe superfamily or fold membership does not justify transferring function, such as annotating an unknown ferritin-like protein as a catalase, RNR or iron store. It does not justify transferring the metal specificity (Fe vs Mn), the oxidant, the radical or non-radical mechanism, or the quaternary structure either. Within a family, close homologs support more reliable inference, but that needs active-site residue conservation, metal-ligand pattern, genomic context, assembly state and experimental biochemistry (metal content, activity assays). Likewise, a template from one family is useful for fold-level modeling of the helical bundle and di-metal core, but not for modeling oligomer interfaces, loops, or ligand and cofactor binding in another family. When choosing representatives, pick them per family and by the function of interest, not by superfamily membership alone. The three should be treated as related by ancestry but functionally distinct. The fold also contains other families, including rubrerythrin and other di-iron/di-manganese proteins, which further show that the scaffold supports diverse chemistry.
